Connect Four Flip · design review
Hardware and Software Technologies for Design · flip board · model v2.1 · 27 Nov 2026

The flip board, ready for review before we build it

This is the complete design of our physical Connect Four Flip board: the 3D model, a simulation of the flip, the clearance check, the wiring and power plan, and how every part is printed and assembled. We are asking for approval to start printing and building. Nothing has been built yet, so everything here is untested on hardware.

7 × 6standard board, 2 players, 42 coins
€55electronics already bought, plus about €11 of PLA
5 print runsabout 48.5 h, 491 g PLA, plus a 2.5 h sensor test first
0 screwsparts click, slide or pin together; no supports

What the game does

Two players drop red and yellow coins into a 7 × 6 board as in normal Connect Four. At the start of each game the system picks a pattern at random: a 4-coin shape that is not a straight line, shown to both players on the app. When a player completes that pattern, the app lights up a Flip button with an animation, and the player chooses Flip or Skip.

A flip turns the whole board upside down. The coins stay in their columns, but each column's order reverses; columns never swap. There is one flip per game. After a flip: if only one player has a line of 4 or more, that player wins; if both do, the player who did not flip wins; if neither does, play continues with no more flips.

How the system works

Coin drops into a column through the sensor bar on top of the board.
Two Hall sensors per column (front and back wall) see the magnet in the coin.
The ESP32 records the column, keeps the game state, checks the rules and the pattern.
The phone app (ProtoPie) shows the board and offers Flip or Skip; it only displays and sends choices.
The servo turns the board 180° directly through its horn. Gates at each end hold the coins in during the flip.

The phone screens can be tried in the App prototype: a board simulator stands in for the physical coins (press 1–7 to drop one). The ESP32 owns the game logic. The app talks to it through ProtoPie Connect on a laptop over USB, with simple MESSAGE||VALUE text lines in both directions. The ESP32 runs from that USB cable; the servo and the 14 sensors run from a 4 × AA battery pack, with all grounds joined. The servo never draws power from the ESP32.

What we ask you to approve

  1. The mechanism. A screw-free printed frame: two uprights in foot sockets on a base, the board hanging between the servo horn on the left and a printed axle pin on the right, and hand-operated sliding gates at both ends. See How it works and Fit check.
  2. The sensing. A magnet in every coin and two A3144 Hall sensors per column in the sensor bar, front and back, so a coin is seen whichever way round it falls.
  3. The wiring and power plan. ESP32 on USB, servo and sensors on 4 × AA, common ground, columns 0–6 on pins D23, D22, D21, D19, D18, D5, D15 and the servo on D4. See Wiring and power.
  4. The print plan. 5 runs of 9 to 11 hours on a printer with at least a 220 × 220 mm bed, after a 2.5-hour test run: the sensor test piece and one test coin. See Print runs and build steps.

Our next step after approval: print the sensor test piece with one test coin, glue in a magnet, and check that the coin is detected reliably. Only then do we start the 5 long runs.

Open points and assumptions

Untested on hardware to test

Fit and clearances are checked on the 3D model by computer (no overlaps; smallest moving gap 0.8 mm). Nothing has been printed, wired or powered yet.

Servo and horn sizes to measure

Assumed from the datasheet class: flange to horn face 16.5 mm, flange to case bottom 28 mm, horn 38 mm long with a 10 mm hub, 5.5 mm arms, 2.8 mm thick. We measure the real servo before printing runs 1 to 4; each value is one number in the model file.

Sensor through the wall to test

Each sensor sits behind a 0.8 mm printed wall. The test run (one sensor test piece and one coin with its magnet) checks that a falling coin switches the sensor every time; if not, we thin the wall before printing the bar.

Servo strength to test

The board turns about its own middle, so the servo mostly works against friction and uneven coin weight. We expect a 13 kg·cm servo to be more than enough, but have not measured the torque.

Lab printer to confirm

The board half is 214.5 mm wide, so the bed must be at least 220 × 220 mm. Times are for a standard printer; we will re-slice with the lab printer's profile.

Snap parts in PLA to confirm

The 4 board clips and the servo strap print in PLA, with spares. If they crack, we reprint them in PETG in one short extra run.

Upright colours decided

To save two print runs, the coins print beside the uprights, so the left upright comes out red and the right one yellow, one colour per player.

Software decided

No code is written yet, by team decision. The message table between the ESP32 and the app is defined; the code comes after the hardware is approved.
